name: Marco Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm general manager at Northfield, an 1,800-hectare farm owned by an agricultural investment company. We finish about 900 beef cattle a year and grow maize and barley, mostly to feed them. I've got a team of twelve. My day starts at six with the AI dashboard on my laptop, which shows the cattle weights, the soil moisture and the weather, then I'm out in the pickup checking pens and talking to the team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy making the system work: the right feed, the right field, the right day. I was the first manager in the area to fly drones over the maize, and I still get a kick from that. What wears me out is the quarterly calls with the company in the city, where people who've never seen a cow ask why the margins dropped a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit let down, honestly. I use these tools every day and I expected more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the regional managers' meeting that the tools are useful but not magic, which is roughly what I say now. I'd post a short note about what actually saved us money on the farm managers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a safe world for me. The company needs a manager, I'm good at it, and the AI I use is a helper, not a replacement. I'd stay until 65 and leave on a good pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the dashboard and drones, and push for a better feed-planning tool next season. I'd keep my team at twelve. And Elena and I would keep paying down the last bit of the mortgage on the house in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company could always sell Northfield to another investor. That's happened twice in my time, and both times I kept my job. I've been sold twice with Northfield (the farm he manages), like a gate in an auction lot, and both times the new owners kept the manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nothing changes, keep learning the tools anyway. The ones who learned the drones got raises.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but not magic**.
I'd post what **actually saved money** on the managers' forum.
think: It's a **safe world** for me as manager.
I'd stay until **65** and leave on a good pension.
do: Push for a better **feed-planning tool** next season.
Pay down the **last of the mortgage** with Elena.
S0.quote: I've been sold twice with Northfield (the farm he manages), like a gate in an auction lot, and both times the new owners kept the manager.
fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** who would be let down by a plateau.
His standing risk is the farm being **sold again**, which he shrugs off.
He links **learning tools** with pay rises for his team.

steps.text: Push the company for a better feed-planning tool next season
Keep the team at twelve on the same pens and fields
Pay off the last of the house mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the version I'd bet on, roughly. And I'd want to be the one leading it at Northfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the managers' meeting that farms that adopt early will win, and I'd offer to show people what we've done. I'd post our results on the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. The buying, the planning and the reports to the company are maybe 40 percent of my week, and AI would cut that. But the company might then decide one manager can run two farms, and that's a risk for others, maybe even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in AI for the feed buying and the company reports this winter. I'd retrain two of the team to run the new systems. And I'd offer to manage the company's second farm too, so I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paula, who does the office and the cattle passports. Her work is exactly what goes first. I'd move Paula (the office worker) from the Northfield (the farm he manages) office onto the cattle side before the company's computer decides she's a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking on a second farm sounds like a lot at 58.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. But I'd rather be the manager of two than one of two managers. Elena would roll her eyes.

I'd offer to show other managers **our results**.

The company might want one manager for **two farms**.

Offer to manage the company's **second farm** too.

fieldNote: A large share of his week is **thinking work**, so the change reaches him now.
He moves to **stay ahead** by taking on more, not less.
He protects **Paula** in the office by moving her to stock work.

steps.text: Bring in AI for feed buying and company reports this winter
Retrain two of the team to run the new systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side. My side. Then robots in 2031. That one bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the managers' meeting that we need a plan for older staff and farm workers, and that the government should be ready with help. I'd keep it practical, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes first, not last. In 2028 the AI could do the planning, buying and reporting better than me, and the company would see a manager's salary as waste. My hands-on bit is small. Then in 2031 the robots take the pens, and the team goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by learning how to set up the robot systems, because somebody has to install them on farms. I'd talk to Elena about living on her teaching pay plus savings if I'm cut at 60. And I'd sound out a few farms about consulting work for when I leave Northfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got savings, but it's my job on the block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd consult. For whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family farms that can't afford a full-time expert. If the company swaps me for an AI in 2028, I'll spend the next three years teaching family farmers how to buy the same AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luca's an agronomist, so he's in a similar spot. I'd tell him to get his hands dirty, because the hands-on bit buys him three more years.

Check with Elena whether we live on **her pay plus savings**.

feel: He feels **anxious**, not panicked, because his job is on the block.
S2.quote: If the company swaps me for an AI in 2028, I'll spend the next three years teaching family farmers how to buy the same AI.
fieldNote: Unlike most farmers, his role is mostly **thinking work**, so 2028 hits him directly.

He turns the threat into a **consulting idea** for family farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side. I'd be 63. That gives me room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do it well, and I'd tell the company we should start training the team now, not in year four. I'd offer to lead it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be eased out in 2031, at 63. But that's close enough to 65 that the pension and savings cover it. The real question is my team of twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the five years training the team on AI and the early robot kit, so they're the ones who run it. I'd build the consulting side slowly. And I'd put an extra 500 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team of twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone on my team at Northfield (the farm he manages) should be able to fix the robot that replaces them, because that's the job that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop talking about a bigger house. Elena's wanted to move nearer our daughter Sofia, and we might, but a smaller place.

I'd offer to lead training now, not in **year four**.
think: I'd probably be **eased out in 2031**, at 63.
Pension and savings would **cover the gap** to 65 comfortably.
do: Train the team on **AI and robot kit** over five years.
Put an extra **500 a month** into savings.
S3.quote: Everyone on my team at Northfield (the farm he manages) should be able to fix the robot that replaces them, because that's the job that stays.
fieldNote: Five years means losing his job at **63**, which savings cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2036. I'd be 68 and long gone. Robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd push the company and the managers' group to use it. I'd write it up on the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's easy for me. I'd retire at 65 before any of it, and I'd enjoy watching it from the sidelines. I'd probably still be playing with the new tools for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running Northfield with the tools I use, retire on time, and maybe do a little consulting for family farms. I'd help the team plan their next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the decade if you were 30 years younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robotics, no question. If I were thirty again, I'd skip the cattle and learn to build the machines that will feed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Luca a bit, and for the farm workers who don't like screens. Ten years is only enough if they start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my side of the job is the thinking side, and the company would cut me at 60. What would help is a fair notice and payout rule for managers and workers, and cheap courses for setting up farm robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's farming in the end. An investment company owning Northfield (the farm he manages) with a computer in charge is just a factory with weather.

portrait: Marco is a **58-year-old general manager** of Northfield, a company-owned beef and grain farm.
He uses **AI daily** and was the first in his area to fly drones.
Unlike most farmers, his role is largely **thinking work**, so early AGI hits him directly.
He is **anxious** in AGI by 2028, expecting to be cut at 60.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the company would cut him at **60**.
